studies.Population: 35,239 men aged 50–76 years residing in western Washington State who were free of prostate cancer at baseline
studies.Ethnicity Basis: Default: no protocol-mapped specific country or population was established
studies.Ethnicity Supporting Text: Participants, 50-76 yr, were 35,239 male members of the VITamins and Lifestyle (VITAL) cohort who were residents of western Washington state
studies.Reference: Specialty supplements and prostate cancer risk in the VITamins and Lifestyle (VITAL) cohort.
studies.Authors: Brasky TM, Kristal AR, Navarro SL, Lampe JW, Peters U, Patterson RE, White E
studies.Timing: Supplement use during the 10 years before baseline; prostate cancer followed from baseline through December 31, 2007, with median follow-up of 6.1 years.
studies.direction_imputation_reason: Comparison direction was not explicit; the protocol assumes high versus low exposure.
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Participants responded about their frequency (days/wk) and duration (yr) of specialty supplement uses.

effect_size.location: Table 2, Associations Between Specialty Supplements and Prostate Cancer Risk

confidence_interval.excerpt: We previously reported no association between use of saw palmetto, typically taken for BPH, and prostate cancer risk in this cohort (HR 0.95, 95% CI: 0.74–1.23) ( 25 ); after an additional 4 years of follow-up, we continue to observe no association.

disease_scope_review.endpoint_excerpt: There were no associations for use of chondroitin, coenzyme Q10, fish oil, garlic, ginkgo biloba, ginseng, glucosamine, or saw palmetto.
disease_scope_review.reason: The chondroitin association concerns the general prostate cancer outcome, not an aggressive subtype.

evidence_scope_projection.definition: Overall prostate cancer evidence, excluding estimates solely about aggressive prostate cancer. General estimates from papers that also report aggressive endpoints remain included. Uncertain endpoints retain their existing review and pooling restrictions.
